ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Soft tissue pathology includes benign and malignant tumors, inflammatory lesions, and metabolic disorders of muscles, fat, and connective tissue. Clinicians must integrate history, exam, and targeted investigations to reach a diagnosis and guide management.

b: Correlate imaging with biopsy when feasible
sections.p: Soft tissue pathology refers to any disease affecting non‑osseous, non‑epithelial structures such as muscle, adipose tissue, tendons, and fascia. Diagnosis combines clinical pattern recognition with imaging and histopathology.
Malignant soft‑tissue sarcomas are staged by size, depth, grade, and presence of metastasis (TNM). Benign lesions are graded by symptom burden and functional impact.

Most soft‑tissue masses are benign (lipoma, fibroma). Malignancy risk rises with rapid growth, deep location, and prior radiation. Infectious causes include bacterial cellulitis, mycobacterial abscess, and parasitic cysts, especially in tropical regions.

Patients notice a painless, enlarging lump; pain, neurovascular compromise, or systemic symptoms suggest aggressive disease or infection. Constitutional signs (fever, weight loss) point to infection or malignancy.
Imaging and tissue sampling clarify the nature of the lesion.

t.b: Cystic → likely benign; solid → further imaging needed
Heterogeneous enhancement suggests malignancy; fat signal indicates lipoma
Confirms sarcoma grade; if unavailable, refer for excisional biopsy

sections.p: Rapid growth, pain, neuro deficits, ulceration, or systemic illness require urgent evaluation. Untreated sarcoma can metastasize; infections can lead to sepsis or compartment syndrome.

b: Wide local excision for sarcoma – clear margins prevent recurrence
Doxorubicin‑based chemo for high‑grade sarcoma – avoids agents with high cardiotoxicity in low‑resource settings
Penicillin for bacterial myositis – covers common organisms
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then address symptoms and functional loss. Surgical excision is primary for most tumors; chemotherapy/radiation for high‑grade sarcomas. Infections need antibiotics or antiparasitics.

b: MRI every 6 months for 2 years after sarcoma resection
Vaccination and antiretroviral therapy reduce opportunistic soft‑tissue infections
sections.p: Regular imaging monitors for recurrence; physiotherapy restores function. Prevent infection by wound care and controlling endemic diseases (TB, HIV).

b: MRI may underestimate depth in obese patients
Inflammatory markers can be normal in early sarcoma
sections.p: Imaging and labs may be deceptive.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly enlarging mass, severe pain, neurovascular loss, fever, weight loss
